pages.x: In May 1967 Egypt's president, Gamal Abdel Nasser, the hero of the Arab world, moved troops into Sinai, sent away the UN peacekeepers there and closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli ships. Arab radio stations promised Israel's destruction, and Israelis feared for their lives. Jordan signed a defence pact with Egypt.

On the morning of 5 June Israel struck first. Its planes, flying low under the radar, destroyed most of Egypt's air force on the ground in three hours, then the air forces of Jordan and Syria. Its tanks raced across Sinai and reached the Suez Canal in four days.

When Jordan joined the fighting, Israeli paratroopers took the Old City of Jerusalem on 7 June and reached the Western Wall, the holiest place where Jews may pray, which had been closed to them since 1948. Israel also took the whole West Bank of the Jordan River.

In the last two days Israel stormed the Golan Heights, the plateau from which Syrian guns had shelled its villages below. A ceasefire on 10 June ended the war. Israel now held more than three times as much land as before.
Some 300,000 Palestinians fled or were driven from the West Bank and Gaza, many for the second time since 1948, and about a million more now lived under Israeli military rule.
pages.of: Palestinians fled or were driven out

pages.x: Meeting in Khartoum in September, Arab leaders said no to peace, to recognition and to talks with Israel. In November the UN Security Council passed Resolution 242, calling on Israel to leave lands it had taken and on every state in the region to live in peace within secure borders. It is still the basis of peace plans.

The war changed the Middle East. Israel gave Sinai back to Egypt for peace in 1982, but it still holds the Golan Heights and East Jerusalem, and its settlements have spread across the West Bank. The lands taken in 1967, and the millions of Palestinians living in them, are at the heart of the conflict to this day.
pts: Israel took Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank and the Golan
All of Jerusalem came under Israeli rule
